notes.definition: The roots, stem and leaves form a plant organ system for the transport of substances around the plant. Water and mineral ions move up the xylem in the transpiration stream, and dissolved sugars move through the phloem by translocation.
explanation: Root hair cells absorb water and mineral ions from the soil. Each root hair cell has a long, thin extension that gives a large surface area. Water moves into the cell by osmosis, because the cell sap is more concentrated than the soil water. Mineral ions are usually more concentrated inside the cell than in the soil, so they are absorbed by active transport, which needs energy from respiration in the cell's many mitochondria.

Xylem tissue is made of hollow tubes strengthened by lignin. It is adapted for the transport of water and dissolved mineral ions from the roots, through the stem, to the leaves in the transpiration stream. Phloem tissue is made of elongated cells with pores in the end walls that allow cell sap to move from one phloem cell to the next. Phloem transports dissolved sugars from the leaves to the rest of the plant for immediate use or for storage. This movement is called translocation, and it can go up or down the plant.

Transpiration is the loss of water vapour from the leaves. Water evaporates from the surfaces of mesophyll cells into the air spaces, then diffuses out through the stomata. This pulls more water up the xylem from the roots, creating a continuous transpiration stream. The stream brings water for photosynthesis and keeps cells turgid, carries mineral ions to the leaves, and evaporation helps cool the leaf. Guard cells control the size of the stomata and so control both gas exchange and water loss.

Four factors affect the rate of transpiration. Higher temperature increases the rate because water molecules have more kinetic energy, so evaporation and diffusion are faster. Lower humidity increases the rate because the concentration gradient of water vapour between the leaf and the air is steeper. More air movement (wind) increases the rate because it blows away water vapour from around the leaf, keeping the gradient steep. Higher light intensity increases the rate because more stomata open to let carbon dioxide in for photosynthesis, so more water vapour can escape.

The rate of transpiration can be estimated with a potometer, which measures the rate of water uptake by a leafy shoot (almost all water taken up is lost by transpiration). As the shoot takes up water, an air bubble moves along a capillary tube. Rate = distance moved ÷ time, or volume of water taken up ÷ time. The volume can be found from the distance moved and the cross-sectional area of the tube (πr² × distance). The stomata on a leaf can be counted by painting nail varnish on the leaf surface, peeling it off and viewing it under a microscope.
keyFacts: Roots, stem and leaves form a plant organ system for transport.
Root hair cells have a large surface area; water enters by osmosis and mineral ions by active transport.
Xylem: hollow tubes strengthened by lignin, carrying water and mineral ions upwards (transpiration stream).
Phloem: elongated cells with pores in end walls, carrying dissolved sugars (translocation) up or down.
Transpiration is the loss of water vapour from leaves, mainly through stomata.
Rate of transpiration increases with higher temperature, lower humidity, more air movement and higher light intensity.
Guard cells open and close stomata to control gas exchange and water loss.
A potometer measures the rate of water uptake, which is used to estimate transpiration rate.
Rate = distance (or volume) ÷ time; volume of water in a tube = πr² × length.

keyTerms.definition: The loss of water vapour from the leaves of a plant by evaporation and diffusion through the stomata.
The continuous movement of water from the roots, up the xylem, to the leaves.
The movement of dissolved sugars through the phloem from the leaves to the rest of the plant.
A root cell with a long extension that increases surface area for absorbing water and mineral ions.
A strong substance that strengthens xylem walls.
Apparatus used to measure the rate of water uptake by a plant shoot.
The amount of water vapour in the air.
Movement of substances against a concentration gradient using energy from respiration.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think plants take in water through their leaves.
misconceptions.right: In fact water is absorbed mainly by root hair cells and moves up the xylem; leaves lose water by transpiration.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think mineral ions are absorbed by osmosis or diffusion.
misconceptions.right: In fact mineral ions are usually absorbed by active transport because they are more concentrated inside root hair cells than in the soil; osmosis refers only to water.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think phloem only moves substances downwards.
misconceptions.right: In fact translocation can move sugars up or down, wherever they are needed for use or storage.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think a potometer directly measures water lost by transpiration.
misconceptions.right: In fact it measures water uptake; a small amount of water is used in photosynthesis or to keep cells turgid, so it is an estimate of transpiration.

realWorld: Farmers growing crops in greenhouses control humidity and ventilation to manage transpiration and prevent wilting.
Florists cut flower stems under water to stop air bubbles blocking the xylem.
Gardeners water plants in the evening when temperature and light intensity are lower, so less water is lost by transpiration.
examTips: For each factor affecting transpiration, explain the effect using evaporation, diffusion, concentration gradient or stomata, not just 'it increases'.
Say 'water vapour diffuses out of the stomata', not 'water diffuses'.
Remember that xylem carries water up only, but phloem can carry sugars up or down.
In potometer calculations, check units: convert minutes to hours, or cm³ to mm³, as asked.
When describing a potometer, mention cutting the shoot under water and sealing joints to keep it airtight.
summary: Roots, stem and leaves form the plant transport organ system.
Root hair cells absorb water by osmosis and mineral ions by active transport.
Xylem carries water and ions up; phloem carries sugars up and down (translocation).
Transpiration is water vapour loss from leaves, pulling water up the xylem.
Temperature, humidity, air movement and light intensity affect transpiration rate.
A potometer measures water uptake: rate = distance or volume ÷ time.

questions.question: Which tissue carries water from the roots to the leaves?
questions.explanation: Xylem carries water and mineral ions upwards.

questions.question: What is the movement of dissolved sugars through a plant called?
questions.explanation: Translocation happens in the phloem. Transpiration is water loss from leaves.

questions.question: How do mineral ions enter root hair cells?
questions.explanation: Ions are usually more concentrated inside the cell, so energy is needed to absorb them by active transport. Osmosis refers only to water.

questions.question: Which change would increase the rate of transpiration?
options: Putting the plant in the dark
questions.explanation: Wind removes water vapour from around the leaf, keeping the concentration gradient steep. The other changes reduce transpiration.

questions.question: Why does transpiration increase in bright light?
options: More stomata open to let carbon dioxide in for photosynthesis
questions.explanation: Open stomata allow more water vapour to diffuse out.

questions.question: What adaptation of phloem allows cell sap to move between cells?
options: A large surface area root hair
questions.explanation: Phloem cells have pores in their end walls (sieve plates) so sap can flow through.

questions.question: Why does high humidity reduce the rate of transpiration?
options: It reduces the concentration gradient of water vapour between the leaf and the air
questions.explanation: Moist air means less difference in water vapour concentration, so diffusion out of the stomata is slower.

questions.question: A potometer actually measures:
options: the rate of water uptake by the shoot
the exact volume of water lost through stomata
questions.explanation: It measures uptake. Most, but not all, of this water is lost by transpiration, so it is an estimate.

questions.question: Why is the shoot cut under water when setting up a potometer?
options: To stop air entering the xylem and blocking water flow
To kill the cells in the stem
questions.explanation: An air bubble in the xylem would break the column of water and stop uptake.

questions.question: Which statement explains why transpiration pulls water up the xylem?
options: Water is pumped up by the phloem
Root pressure alone pushes water to the top of tall trees
As water evaporates and diffuses out of the leaves, more water is drawn up the xylem to replace it
questions.explanation: Loss of water from leaves creates a continuous pull on the water column in the xylem (transpiration stream).

questions.question: Which feature increases the surface area of a root for absorbing water?
questions.explanation: Root hairs are long extensions that greatly increase the surface area in contact with soil water.

questions.question: The bubble in a potometer moved 48 mm in 6 minutes. Calculate the rate of water uptake in mm/min.
questions.explanation: rate = distance ÷ time = 48 ÷ 6 = 8 mm/min.

questions.question: A plant took up 3.6 cm³ of water in 1.5 hours. Calculate the rate of water uptake in cm³ per hour.
questions.explanation: 3.6 ÷ 1.5 = 2.4 cm³ per hour.

questions.question: A potometer capillary tube has a radius of 0.5 mm. The bubble moved 25 mm in 2 minutes. Calculate the rate of water uptake in mm³/min. Use π = 3.14.
questions.explanation: Find the cross-sectional area, multiply by distance to get volume, then divide by time. 19.625 ÷ 2 = 9.8125, about 9.81 mm³/min.

questions.question: The rate of water uptake was 12 mm³/min in still air and 30 mm³/min with a fan. Calculate the percentage increase.
A plant loses water at a rate of 15 mm³ per minute. Calculate the volume lost in 4 hours in cm³.
questions.explanation: 4 hours = 240 minutes. 15 × 240 = 3600 mm³. Since 1 cm³ = 1000 mm³, this is 3.6 cm³.

questions.question: State what is meant by transpiration.
markScheme: 1 mark: the loss of water (vapour) from the leaves (through the stomata)
questions.explanation: Transpiration is evaporation and diffusion of water vapour out of leaves.

questions.question: Name the tissue that carries sugars and state where the sugars are made.
questions.explanation: Sugars made in the leaves are translocated through the phloem.

questions.question: Explain how a root hair cell is adapted to absorb water.
markScheme: 1 mark: long thin root hair gives a large surface area
1 mark: water moves in by osmosis from the dilute soil water to the more concentrated cell sap
questions.explanation: Surface area and the water potential (concentration) difference together allow fast water uptake.

questions.question: Explain why increasing temperature increases the rate of transpiration.
markScheme: 1 mark: water molecules gain more kinetic energy
1 mark: so evaporation from cells and diffusion of water vapour out of the stomata is faster
questions.explanation: More energy means faster evaporation and diffusion.

questions.question: Describe how a student could use a potometer to measure the rate of water uptake by a leafy shoot.
markScheme: 1 mark: cut the shoot under water and fit it into the potometer so it is airtight
1 mark: introduce an air bubble and measure the distance it moves along the scale in a set time
1 mark: calculate rate = distance ÷ time; reset the bubble using the reservoir and repeat
questions.explanation: Key points are setting up without air leaks, measuring bubble movement over time, and repeating.

questions.question: Explain why the rate of transpiration increases on a windy day.
markScheme: 1 mark: wind blows water vapour away from the leaf surface
1 mark: so the concentration of water vapour outside the leaf stays low / the concentration gradient remains steep
1 mark: so water vapour diffuses out of the stomata faster
questions.explanation: Without wind, a layer of moist air builds up near the leaf, reducing the gradient.

questions.question: Explain why root hair cells contain many mitochondria and why this is necessary.
markScheme: 1 mark: mineral ions are absorbed by active transport
1 mark: because they move against a concentration gradient (lower concentration in soil than in cell)
1 mark: active transport needs energy from respiration, which happens in mitochondria
questions.explanation: The number of mitochondria reflects the cell's energy demand for absorbing ions.

questions.question: Give one reason why a plant needs water.
markScheme: 1 mark: any one: photosynthesis; keeping cells turgid / support; transporting mineral ions; cooling the leaves
questions.explanation: Water is needed for several processes, so any correct one scores.

questions.question: Describe how water moves from the soil to the air around a leaf.
markScheme: Indicative content: water enters root hair cells by osmosis; root hairs give a large surface area; water moves across the root to the xylem; travels up the xylem (hollow tubes strengthened with lignin) in the stem in the transpiration stream; reaches leaves; evaporates from mesophyll cell surfaces into air spaces; water vapour diffuses out through stomata (transpiration); loss of water pulls more water up the xylem.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): clear sequence from root hair to stomata with correct processes named (osmosis, evaporation, diffusion).
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): some correct steps or structures with gaps or errors in sequence.
questions.explanation: Name each process at the right stage: osmosis in the root, flow in the xylem, evaporation and diffusion in the leaf.

questions.question: A student uses a potometer to investigate how air movement and light intensity affect the rate of transpiration. Describe a method the student could use, and explain the results they would expect for both factors.
markScheme: Indicative content: method: cut shoot under water, set up potometer airtight, dry leaves; allow to acclimatise; measure distance bubble moves in a fixed time (for example 5 minutes); vary air movement using a fan at different distances or settings, or light intensity using a lamp at different distances; control other variables: temperature (use a heat shield or water bath, same room), humidity, same shoot, same leaf area; repeat readings and calculate mean; calculate rate (distance or volume ÷ time). Expected results and explanations: more air movement increases rate because water vapour is blown away, maintaining a steep concentration gradient so diffusion is faster; higher light intensity increases rate because more stomata open for photosynthesis, so more water vapour diffuses out; rate may level off when stomata are fully open.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): detailed, workable method with control variables and repeats, plus correct explanations for both factors.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): reasonable method with some control variables and an explanation for at least one factor.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple method or predictions with little explanation.
questions.explanation: Separate the method from the explanations. Mention controlling temperature when using a lamp because lamps can heat the shoot.

questions.question: Which organs make up the plant transport organ system?
questions.explanation: Roots, stem and leaves are organs; xylem and phloem are tissues within them.

questions.question: In which direction can translocation move sugars?
questions.explanation: Sugars are moved to wherever they are needed, for example up to growing shoots or down to roots for storage.
